> Extended support for both 7 and 8.1 ended years ago (even paid support for embedded POS editions, so there's no way to get security updates anymore).

I checked the dates to make them explicit:

- [Windows 7](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/lifecycle/products/windows-7) is EOL for mainstream since Jan 13, 2015, extended support ended on Jan 14, 2020, and paid extended++ support ended on Jan 10, 2023.
- [Windows 8.1](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/lifecycle/products/windows-81) is EOL for mainstream since Jan 9, 2018, and extended support ended on Jan 10, 2023. Not other paid extension.

> Windows 7 market shared according to [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/hwsurvey) - 0.12%, Windows 8/8.1 are not on the list.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/06f9fefd-d8e8-4122-9d96-3d09bb3e9738)

The sum of the 3 listed versions is 96.05%, while the Windows share is reported as 96.10%, so we can assume Windows 8/8.1 are the remaining 0.05%. Unless Steam somehow still works on Windows XP :P

---

So yeah, I think it's time to say goodbye to Windows < 10, even though I still feel Windows 10 is the new kid on the block :sweat_smile:

This is really disappointing to see to me, Godot's ability to run on older machines was something that I really enjoyed. Why not just have the stuff that requires AccessKit not work on OS that do not support it? I understand that not many people use these old OS, but Godot's support for them was really noble to me.

> Why not just have the stuff that requires AccessKit not work on OS that do not support it?

It was done in multiple previous cases (e.g., in the case of DX12), when it was reasonably easy to do without compromising functionality, but this time there's no straightforward way to do it, since affected code is part of a third-party library.

> > Why not just have the stuff that requires AccessKit not work on OS that do not support it?
> 
> It was done in multiple previous cases (e.g., in the case of DX12), when it was reasonably easy to do without compromising functionality, but this time there's no straightforward way to do it, since affected code is part of a third-party library.

I don't think I'll be able to change anyone's minds, which makes sense given how old these OS are, but, at the very least, is it possible to support these old OS only if the engine is compiled with the accesskit disabled build option?

> is it possible to support these old OS only if the engine is compiled with the accesskit disabled build option?

This means keeping (maintaining, and updating when new features are added) a lot of unneeded, messy code.

> This is really disappointing to see to me, Godot's ability to run on older machines was something that I really enjoyed. Why not just have the stuff that requires AccessKit not work on OS that do not support it? I understand that not many people use these old OS, but Godot's support for them was really noble to me.

Install linux.
Windows 7 should not be used in 2025, as stated, support ended in 2015, that's 10 years.

> > This is really disappointing to see to me, Godot's ability to run on older machines was something that I really enjoyed. Why not just have the stuff that requires AccessKit not work on OS that do not support it? I understand that not many people use these old OS, but Godot's support for them was really noble to me.
> 
> Install linux. Windows 7 should not be used in 2025, as stated, support ended in 2015, that's 10 years.

It's not about what I actively use, even though I did use win7 until 2023, I just liked the way godot made itself widely available and compatible for old systems.

It doesn't *need* to, but it was really nice that it did. I'm considering not updating my game past 4.5-dev2 because I really, really like having my game be playable on as many different systems as possible - even when it isn't explicitly necessary.

I just know there has to be more ways other than dropping compatibility entirely, and I think that this PR should be reconsidered. There's many others like me who take pride in having support for legacy systems, and it made me really happy that godot supported this.

Iirc, Steam ended support for 8.1 and older systems recently, so that's probably why there's no data about those systems in it's reports. Take in consideration the less financially privileged people who will be gatekept from using the engine AND playing the game made in it.

I'd say any computer that can *only* run pre-Win 8 is very badly suited to use Godot 4.x, and I'd say anyone limited in that way should run a Linux variant instead, running a deeply insecure version of Windows isn't something I think we should support or encourage when there are safer alternatives

Additional data from [StatCounter](https://gs.statcounter.com/windows-version-market-share/desktop/worldwide/#monthly-202505-202505-bar) says that Windows 8/8.1 use is under 0.5%, Windows 7 is apparently at ~2.5%, but I highly doubt that market share is relevant for development. It seems Windows 7 is much lower in most regions, with China probably being the main driver of the stats
Thanks!

Thanks for the work done, but I don't quite understand how you can change the legendary OC to a screen reader... Despite all the above arguments, and the lack of security, for example, I recently read that the Win7 market is still pretty strong, to the surprise of Microsoft themselves. We have a lot of problems with CPU and GPU particles, in the sense that Godot tries to support the same capabilities and functionality for both particles, the same applies to rendering methods, but we somehow bypass and cope with this, probably many will have to stay on version 4.4, which is not very good.
Given the abnormal amount of push-back against this, I _really_ think this should be reconsidered. I obviously am very biased though.

> I don't quite understand how you can change the legendary OC to a screen reader...

The what?

>  We have a lot of problems with CPU and GPU particles, in the sense that Godot tries to support the same capabilities and functionality for both particles, the same applies to rendering methods, but we somehow bypass and cope with this, probably many will have to stay on version 4.4, which is not very good.

These are hardware features, it's not the same as an outdated OS. As said multiple times, an updated, safe, modern version of linux can run on old hardware, the same cannot be said of Windows.
Windows 11 doesn't run on 7th gen intel, and Windows 10 doesn't run on Windows 7 PCs. And around 7th gen is the least you need to run godot, like they have in my universitys computers.

even a phone or chromebook is far more powerful than a Windows 7 PC.

I don't think this has any significant evidence of pushback, far from abnormal, and the change is pretty straight forward so:
* If there *is* more pushback as we go forward we can easily revert it (and improve the hacky code)
* People can restore the code themselves to keep this unsupported case
I'd like to hear the pushback, though. If there are other avenues where this PR has been discussed, by all means, do share.
The good new is 4.5 beta1 still starting with VxKex enabled.

I use Godot 4 on an old Windows 7 Laptop when traveling offline. I never had any issue with working in Godot 4 until now. This laptop is running flawlessly, I don't want to change a thing about it. In fact, being able to do this without having to buy new hardware or completely dump other software I have installed on it, was the reason I chose Godot.

Unlike newer Windows version, Win 7 is a good and very stable OS. I'm pretty sure I'm not the only one who still has hardware with it, especially Laptops, not connected to the Internet and therefore not showing up in statistics. In my personal life,I do know quite a few. I don't want to completely change a perfectly running system and give up on established workflows when working away from home and I can't afford to buy equally powerful new hardware which can run modern Windows versions.

Does this mean that the editor won't support Windows 7, or that the games also won't support Windows 7? In the latter case, knowing a fair amount of people without the means or ability to upgrade from 7, quite a shame, although I know the policy of the project has always been "for older systems use Godot 3 instead" which is understandable from a maintenance cost perspective.
I think editor and using default windows export template will not support Windows 7.
I tested a bunch and the latest Godot 4.5 release version which works under Windows 7 is Godot 4.5 dev 2.
4.5 beta 2 still working with VxKex enabled

> 4.5 beta 2 still working with VxKex enabled

Do I have to build Godot to enable VxKex? Or can I use a command line option when running an official release? If so I can't find it here: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/editor/command_line_tutorial.html

If it is the former, I never build Godot. How would I enable VxKex during the build process?
It's an external tool to run Windows 10/11 apps on Windows 7 - https://github.com/YuZhouRen86/VxKex-NEXT, you do not need to rebuild Godot.
VxKex is interessing because you don't need to rebuild anything...

> I'd say any computer that can _only_ run pre-Win 8 is very badly suited to use Godot 4.x

You're wrong. Godot isn't just for games - I use it as a cross-platform GUI framework, and it works great even on low-end machines running Windows 7. A year ago, I moved my project to Godot 4 to make use of the new features, and now I'm really disappointed that support for Windows 7 is being dropped. A fairly large share of my users still use Windows 7.

I find it hard to understand how the decision was made to sacrifice Windows 7 support in favor of AccessKit. Steam statistics are just that - Steam statistics. There are many users who don’t use Steam at all. But even if we take Steam statistics as a reference, it's important to consider that Steam has over 120 million users, with around 30 million online at any given time. With such a large user base, even 0.12% represents a significant number of people.

> I find it hard to understand how the decision was made to sacrifice Windows 7 support in favor of AccessKit.

@PaulArgent it's quite simple. A person using Windows 7 _chooses_ to use Windows 7 (beyond all reason). They can easily switch to a stable version of Linux that will have continued security updates and will run as well if not better than Windows. But for reasons that are there own, they choose to take the risk and stick with Windows 7. 

On the other hand, a blind person cannot use Godot without screen reader support, which accesskit provides. It is the first step in making Godot truly accessible. 

We never promised continued support for Windows 7. Once it went EOL it became a "best efforts" supported platform. Which ultimately means when something important conflicts with continued support, we would drop it. And that's exactly what happened. 

That's not even mentioning the fact that no contributors have access to Windows 7 devices anymore. Trying to maintain a platform you don't have access to is an exercise in futility.

> They can easily switch to a stable version of Linux that will have continued security updates and will run as well if not better than Windows.

@clayjohn You are proposing a solution that you have never tested yourselves, and you show little consideration for average users. Let’s set aside the general challenges an ordinary user faces when switching to Linux, as well as the inherent technical complexity of reinstalling an operating system. I have tested numerous Linux distributions with the lightest possible desktop environments, such as LXDE or Xfce, on low-end hardware, and the performance was consistently poor-lagging at every step - whereas Windows 7 runs smoothly on the same machines.

Furthermore, you completely disregard the context of schools and universities, where hardware is rarely updated and most educational software is developed specifically for Windows. I once participated in a pilot project aimed at transitioning an educational institution to Linux, and the initiative ultimately failed because Wine could not properly run all the necessary software.

As for the claim that none of the participants have access to devices running Windows 7 - this is disingenuous, as there are numerous virtual machine solutions available for testing purposes. Moreover, no one is asking for exhaustive testing on an outdated OS. All that users like myself are requesting is the preservation of compatibility.

Regarding AccessKit, I fully understand the importance of accessibility. However, it would have been entirely possible to implement AccessKit without dropping support for older systems. Yes, it would have been slightly more complex, but instead, the Godot team opted for the simplest solution, at the expense of an entire segment of users.

Can you provide some evidence of schools and universities that use Windows 7?

But saying that this shows a lack of regard for average users is strange, the overwhelming majority of users do not use Windows 7, so how is that average? And why are you assuming we haven't tested this? I've used Linux on various old hardware instead of reinstalling Windows

We can't reasonably provide support for an OS we cannot and will not test on, that would be hugely irresponsible

I prefer not to share private information here, but quite a few schools in my country still rely on Windows 7. And it's not just about schools. When it comes to hardware, it's likely we have very different definitions of what qualifies as "old hardware" and "low-end hardware." Computers in educational institutions typically combine both characteristics: "old low-end hardware."

In any case, I understand that the decision to drop Windows 7 support is final. At this point, the only viable options are to freeze the engine version for certain projects or, if new functionality is needed in the future, maintain a custom build. I'm genuinely grateful that Godot is open source and that such flexibility is possible.

The very viable option is also VxKex unless it doesn't work on your setup

But also, from just the issue reports on GitHub there's under 1400 total issues reported that has "windows 7" or "win 7" mentioned in them, that's a vanishingly small portion

So to add to the reason behind this:
The addition of access kit broke Windows 7 support, so there were only really two options:
* Drop Windows 7 support
* Try to fix it by guesswork and hope it fixes the problem, as we can't test any solution

The latter is quite obviously really irresponsible, in addition to having significantly reduced feature support by not having access kit

For the future and Windows 10 I'd expect we will support Windows 10 the same way we did with Windows 7, for as long as it is possible and reasonable to do so, i.e. for as long as we can either test it directly, or confirm that it works. Windows 10 enters EOL for base level users in October, and will receive extended and security updates until a year after that. Then it will have extended support for schools and similar until 2028, which I'd say would be the earliest point we could consider dropping support, some enterprise solutions (which I don't think either our maintainers or most expected users will have access to) will only end in 2032, which would be equivalent to last year in the Windows 7 cycle.

If someone was willing to re-implement and maintain support for these platforms, would their contributions be accepted?
And a question about AccessKit - what was it that broke compatibility? Is it not able to be disabled at runtime if a system does not support it?

The issue is that code added to work around issues with running on Windows 7 doesn't work with access kit, so to support running on Windows 7 that needs to be done in a way that supports both

Afaik AccessKit doesn't work on windows 7 regardless
It probably needs some other work arround that VxKex seems to already have... But I don't know how to test if AccessKit is working.

> If someone was willing to re-implement and maintain support for these platforms, would their contributions be accepted?

It's not about maintaining specific Windows 7 code. Keeping it creates unneeded overhead for every contributor, since every future change should be checked for compatibility and new workarounds added, and this is just a waste of time. The whole point of this PR is to remove old code, if we wanted to keep some support it in some capacity we could just leave it as a compile flag like it was before.

To add to what @PaulArgent wrote, computers available to people in libraries, hospital reading rooms etc. are often both old and low-powered. Just before the pandemic, the place where I go for physio offered... Windows XP. No, I am not kidding.

(They stopped offering inpatient physio because pandemic and later Ukraine war, so I have no clue if they upgraded since then, and/or to what)
For old computers, there's LTS 3.x branch that is maintained and is not removing support for Windows 7.

Note that Windows 7 market share is dropping, as of July this year it's now just over 2%, 8 is 0.88% and 8.1 is 0.23% (source [statcounter](https://gs.statcounter.com/windows-version-market-share/desktop/worldwide/#monthly-202507-202507-bar))

Together this change affects barely over 3% of Windows users

If we look at an average over the whole year Jan-July the stats are instead: 2.26% for 7, 0.33% for 8, and 0.28% for 8.1, for a total of 2.87% for these three in total, under 3% (source [statcounter](https://gs.statcounter.com/windows-version-market-share/desktop/worldwide/#monthly-202501-202507-bar))

For the same period all Windows versions make up 25.81% of the total OS market, which isn't necessarily representative of Godot users but I think the 3% for Windows 7 through 8.1 is much higher than the users for these in 4.x so it's more of a rough estimate. But that results in under 1% of the total market being Windows 7 through 8.1 when taken as part of the whole OS market (source [statcounter](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-market-share#monthly-202501-202507-bar))

IMO, the solution is quite simple: If you want to use Godot on Windows 7, use Godot 4.4.x or earlier, not Godot 4.5 or later.

We should probably mark Godot 4.4 as an LTS release for this reason, and keep cherry-picking security fixes, platform support fixes, and minor bug fixes when needed. To be clear, I'm not saying that we should dedicate lots of time and money to this, just a few hours a month of merging in [dedicated cherry-pick PRs](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pulls?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Apr+milestone%3A4.4) and [performing the cherry-pick process](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pulls?q=is%3Apr+label%3Acherrypick%3A4.4+).

EDIT: This was discussed internally and there won't be any special LTS status for Godot 4.4.
IMO, using VxKex and recompiling Windows export template is better option for the moment
Is there no compatible solution to choose from? Most computers require support for Windows 7. I hope there can be a compatibility solution, even if it involves self-compiling or modifying the code.

The changes done in this PR specifically are relatively few and self-contained. One could fork the Godot repository, revert the changes, disable the AccessKit support, and compile their own version of the engine. This is not guaranteed to work, especially in the foreseeable future, but it may serve as a good point of reference.

> Note that Windows 7 market share is dropping, as of July this year it's now just over 2%, 8 is 0.88% and 8.1 is 0.23% (source [statcounter](https://gs.statcounter.com/windows-version-market-share/desktop/worldwide/#monthly-202507-202507-bar))

Keep in mind that the market share does not differentiate between Windows Server and client releases, so chances are the higher market shares for 8.x are likely predominantly stemming from machines running server versions, of which NT 6.2/6.3 still have Windows Server Premium Assurance ESU support up through Oct '26 (NT6.0/NT6.1 have ESU support up through Jan '26). The people that hold onto Vista, 7 and 8.x client are _all_ using hacked-up server update releases offered via the Premium Assurance program. Those usage numbers will drop sharply after the cutoff dates for both Win2k8 (R2) and Win2k12 (R2).

I also have my reservations about application compatibility since most modern-day Windows apps are clearly targeting Windows SDK builds 19041 (v2004) through 26100 (v24H2/25H2). As you target newer SDK releases, you run the risk of breaking compat with older OSes simply because they do not implement the corresponding API sets, so it's either do or die here. Not to mention the increased security risks involved in running an ancient OS from 2007/2009... _Ick._

I'm all for killing support for these OS releases, these are a serious maintenance burden to deal with.

So that this is fully clear:
We did *not* drop the support for Windows 7/8/8.1 because we just decided to not support it any longer

We dropped support because it was always supported on a best effort basis, as long as the engine worked on Windows 7/8/8.1 we would keep supporting those version, but the addition of access kit support meant that the compatibility code for those versions no longer worked

This meant that we had three options:
* Fix it properly, ensuring it works
* Try to fix it "by ear", fixing the support code based on guesses of how it *should* work, but not verifying the fix
* Drop support

In order to do the first option we would need maintainers to test this on Windows 7/8/8.1 machines, but no maintainer has such a setup available, and it's hard to justify installing a *very unsafe* operating system to support this (and ensure other details of it functioning), nor can we really reasonably expect users to do the same, assuming we can consider unsupervised testing by maintainers to be sufficient to guarantee support

The second option is clearly unprofessional, and would most likely lead to bug reports that we simply cannot fix without doing it properly anyway

I was not part of the decision making process myself, but I assume that the decision was made weighing the benefits and costs, and estimates of the number of users relying on these versions, including that, for example, games can't be published on Steam for Windows 7, which also indicates that the target audience for that version is going to be limited as well

Users will try to use your software regardless. You get to choose whether that's on the original OS, or an OS version with a third-party compatibility layer injected into your process, in which case you're inadvertently running against two different Windows API implementations; Microsoft's and one with missing pieces scavenged from ReactOS. At least when the fallbacks are in your own code, you can be confident they behave as you expect.

How many bug reports do you want to deal with where the user says they're on 10 because they've learned developers WONTFIX otherwise but lying sometimes gets results (or, that *other users* will bully them if they don't lie)? Where the API's been modified to report itself as 10 as part of the third-party compatibility layer because of all the software that refuses to run after performing a hard-coded version check? And where you can't reproduce the reported bug because it's inadvertently caused by said unofficial API extension?

I'd hypothesize that the maintenance cost of old compatibility code may well be less than the maintenance cost of spurious bug reports from unsupported platforms. I might be wrong, but this is something I'd hope could be settled using hard data rather than mere statements one way or the other.

On options for how to deal with old Windows versions, there's a fourth: Tell users that if they can get AccessKit working on 7, you'll leave the old compatibility code in. That passes the burden onto the people who care, to either do it themselves or pay someone with the necessary skills for their time.

And finally, to nitpick: There are still numerous Steam users on older Windows versions; I've been lurking a forum thread where a bunch hang out. Some of them use a third-party compatibility layer to run the latest Steam client. Others use the final working version, but have to use either Valve's own command-line tool or a third-party tool to install games/updates, since Steam started using a compression algorithm not implemented in the last compatible GUI. Some just play their existing library, and hope none of the games get a patch they can't download, or outright block Steam from checking for game updates. Even if Steam doesn't let you declare the game compatible with out-of-support OSs (does it?), that doesn't mean the audience there is actually zero people. Try searching the Silksong steam forum for example; there's a thread with at least a handful of users asking whether it works on Windows 7, at least one of whom found a successful workaround, and that game is brand new! It *would* be fair to say the market segment is tiny and almost certainly shrinking with each passing month, though.

> How many bug reports do you want to deal with where the user says they're on 10 because they've learned developers WONTFIX otherwise but lying sometimes gets results (or, that other users will bully them if they don't lie)?

Looking at a current issue stats, about 2-3 in a year, the probability that VxKex will cause a Windows 7 specific issue is quite low. The absolute majority of Windows 7 related issues are issues with ancient GPU/driver, and for such issues Windows version is pretty much irrelevant.

> On options for how to deal with old Windows versions, there's a fourth: Tell users that if they can get AccessKit working on 7, you'll leave the old compatibility code in. That passes the burden onto the people who care, to either do it themselves or pay someone with the necessary skills for their time.

It won't pass the burden onto the people who care. This will require all future changes to be Windows 7 compatible, so this will create an extra burden for everyone. The whole point of this PR is to make it clear that new contributions do not need to bother with Windows 7 compatibility.

Making AccessKit work on Windows 7 is non-trivial, since [Rust dropped Windows 7/8 support a year ago](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2024/05/02/Rust-1.78.0/#compatibility-notes) and a bunch of AccessKit dependencies require newer Rust versions. And it's an actively developed library, so every update will need more and more changes to keep Windows 7 support.

Also, AccessKit is not the only reason for dropping support, it's just a last one, dropping support was considered multiple times before, when DX12 was added and in a few other cases.

> There are still numerous Steam users on older Windows versions;

Most of them are likely relying on UpdatePack7, a compilation of pirated Windows Server 2008 R2 updates, and the last tire of extended security updates for in will end in January. So the numbers will drop greatly.

I think the best solution is to make it so things like AccessKit aren't used at runtime if the platform doesn't support them. Like how headless mode works for rendering, the game still runs, just with rendering stuff returning dummy values.
nevermind

> Making AccessKit work on Windows 7 is non-trivial, since [Rust dropped Windows 7/8 support a year ago](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2024/05/02/Rust-1.78.0/#compatibility-notes)

I'm familiar with Rust. In particular, familiar enough to know that they kept a `i686-win7-windows-msvc` target, and more recently added a `-gnu` as well. You need to explicitly install that version of the toolchain through rustup, and they don't provide a build of the *compiler itself* that runs on older Windows, but even recent Rust versions have a compatibility target. Now, if your argument is "AccessKit doesn't compile when targeting \*-win7-\*" (has anyone tested?), then fair enough.

It obviously won't build, since it's using a newer API. But even if it would, using tier3 (untested) target is not a reasonable option. The point remains the same, nothing is developed with this target in mind, and will require an ever increasing number of changes to keep working.

I would like to remind the community that anyone is welcome to maintain a fork of Godot which works on older systems, such as Windows 7, or potentially even older, through any mechanism (AccessKit on tier3 platform, no AccessKit, etc).

Yes, someone can maintain a fork. Who will use it? It's the tyranny of defaults, cascading down the supply chain. A fix that would be simple upstream becomes a request that must be made to hundreds of direct dependencies to use a non-default option (or, in this case, a plea to each game developer to use a fork rather than the official engine). You know how one of the arguments for why companies would contribute back to open source projects is that it's easier to upstream a change once than continuously re-apply your patches to an internal modified copy? Telling someone to fork off is pretty much equivalent to the swear it blatantly alludes to.

In this case, Godot is far downstream of the project that made an incompatible default, but it is the *final* open-source step before closed-source game developers. This is the only remaining place that the parts of the community who care *can* attempt to contribute back, and maintain an OS-inclusive default.

I believe I saw someone say that the old compatibility code was ugly? Then what level of quality would a replacement need in order to be accepted back?

I would use it if there are advantages over using official build with VxKex... But for the moment no major issues using 4.5.stable and I upgraded a lot of old tutorials projects...

I had a minor issue with Blender 4.5.3 --version flag but Blender 4.3 is ok
